questions.question: What does a rhyme scheme record in a stanza?
options: The poet’s arrangement of punctuation marks
The sequence of stressed and unstressed feet
The number of syllables in every word
The pattern of matching end sounds represented by letters
questions.explanation: A rhyme scheme tracks end-rhyme relationships. The first distinct rhyme is A, the next B, and so on.

questions.question: Four lines end in light, day, night, and play, in that order. What is their rhyme scheme?
questions.explanation: Light rhymes with night (A), and day rhymes with play (B), producing ABAB.

questions.question: A quatrain ends with stone, clear, near, and alone. Which rhyme scheme fits these endings?
questions.explanation: Stone and alone share rhyme A; clear and near share rhyme B. Their order is ABBA.

questions.question: A four-line stanza ends with rain, train, bell, shell. Which scheme results?
questions.explanation: The first two endings rhyme with each other, and the last two form a different rhyme pair: AABB.

questions.question: A four-line ballad-like stanza ends with flame, night, shore, bright. Which rhyme scheme does it show?
questions.explanation: Only night and bright rhyme. Flame and shore each introduce a separate ending sound, so the pattern is ABCB.

questions.question: Six original lines end with light, snow, bright, glow, sea, free. Which label sequence is correct?
questions.explanation: Light/bright form A, snow/glow form B, and sea/free form C; therefore the sequence is ABABCC.

questions.question: Eight line endings run sky, flame, high, shore, name, more, rain, train. Which is the full rhyme scheme?
questions.explanation: Sky/high are A; flame/name B; shore/more C; rain/train D. The order is ABACBCDD.

questions.question: A quatrain uses ABBA end rhyme. If only its third and fourth line endings exchange places, what scheme follows?
questions.explanation: The original sequence A-B-B-A becomes A-B-A-B when the third and fourth endings are exchanged.

questions.question: Which description defines traditional English blank verse?
options: Unrhymed lines with no regular metre
questions.explanation: Blank verse keeps the five-beat iambic pattern but does not use a fixed end-rhyme scheme.

questions.question: Which major work is widely written in blank verse?
options: Alexander Pope’s The Rape of the Lock
questions.explanation: Paradise Lost is predominantly unrhymed iambic pentameter, the defining structure of English blank verse.

questions.question: An English poem has no end rhymes, but its lines generally contain five iambic feet. What is the best classification?
questions.explanation: A consistent five-iamb rhythm without end rhyme points to blank verse rather than free verse.

questions.question: Which feature would DISQUALIFY an otherwise regular iambic-pentameter passage from being blank verse?
questions.explanation: Blank verse permits metrical variation, pauses, and enjambment; a systematic end-rhyme scheme makes it rhymed verse instead.

questions.question: Consider the claims about a 14-line poem: I. Every line follows iambic pentameter. II. Its ends rhyme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. III. It is blank verse because it has five iambs per line. Which judgment is correct?
options: All three are correct because rhyme does not matter in blank verse.
I is false because iambic pentameter cannot occur in a sonnet.
II proves the poem is free verse rather than rhymed metre.
I and II may be true, but III is false because the lines rhyme.
questions.explanation: Regular iambic pentameter can occur in both rhymed and unrhymed poetry; the stated sonnet rhyme pattern rules out blank verse.

questions.question: Which feature most clearly identifies free verse?
options: No obligation to follow a fixed metrical pattern
Exactly five iambic feet in every line
A mandatory rhymed couplet at the end
questions.explanation: Free verse permits the poet to shape rhythm without adhering to a prescribed recurring metre.

questions.question: Which technique can still give free verse a sense of musical rhythm?
options: Exactly ten syllables in every line
Deliberate line breaks, repetition, and natural speech cadence
Identical end rhymes in every line
questions.explanation: Free verse can create audible rhythm through phrasing and repetition without a fixed metrical scheme.

questions.question: Which statement about free verse is the most accurate?
options: All free-verse lines must contain exactly three unstressed syllables.
Free verse must eliminate all sonic devices, including alliteration.
Occasional rhyme may occur, but no regular rhyme-and-metre plan governs the whole poem.
Every free-verse stanza ends in a heroic couplet.
questions.explanation: Free verse may contain echoes of rhyme and rhythmic pattern, but it is not committed to an established regular scheme.

questions.question: A poet uses unequal line lengths, speech-like pauses, and variable stresses, without a repeated metrical design. Which form fits best?
questions.explanation: Variable lengths and cadences with no sustained metrical grid characterize free verse.

questions.question: Two unrhymed passages are compared. Passage A consistently follows five iambs per line; Passage B varies the number and arrangement of stresses. Which distinction is sound?
options: A is blank verse; B may be free verse.
Both must be free verse because neither rhymes.
A is ottava rima; B is rhyme royal.
Both must be blank verse because neither rhymes.
questions.explanation: End rhyme alone does not decide the form: A has regular iambic pentameter, whereas B lacks the sustained metrical pattern.

questions.question: What is the standard metrical and rhyming form of a heroic couplet?
options: Two successive rhyming lines of iambic pentameter
Two unrhymed lines of iambic tetrameter
Four lines with ABBA end rhyme
Three lines with ABA end rhyme
questions.explanation: A heroic couplet consists of a pair of adjacent iambic-pentameter lines that rhyme with one another.

questions.question: Which eighteenth-century poet is especially associated with polished heroic couplets?
questions.explanation: Alexander Pope regularly used balanced, rhymed iambic-pentameter pairs in Augustan poetry.

questions.question: What chiefly distinguishes a heroic couplet from a pair of consecutive blank-verse lines?
options: Only blank verse can contain iambic pentameter.
A heroic couplet always has six stresses per line.
The heroic couplet has end rhyme; blank verse does not.
Blank verse is normally made of three-line stanzas.
questions.explanation: Both can use iambic pentameter, but the heroic couplet has linked end rhymes and blank verse does not.

questions.question: A passage contains four successive iambic-pentameter lines rhyming AABB. How are these lines organised?
questions.explanation: In AABB, lines 1–2 rhyme and lines 3–4 rhyme, giving two consecutive five-beat rhyming pairs.

questions.question: Two rhyming iambic-pentameter lines form a complete sentence that stops at the second line. What makes this a CLOSED heroic couplet?
options: The second line must be an alexandrine.
The syntax and sense reach a clear grammatical close at the end of the pair.
The two lines have no end rhyme.
The sentence must continue into the next couplet.
questions.explanation: A closed couplet contains a complete grammatical unit; enjambment beyond the pair would make it open instead.

questions.question: How many lines form a couplet?
questions.explanation: A couplet is a two-line verse unit, most commonly linked by end rhyme.

questions.question: Which rhyme pattern consists of two consecutive rhyming couplets?
questions.explanation: The first two lines share rhyme A and the next two share rhyme B, forming two pairs.

questions.question: What feature makes a couplet CLOSED rather than OPEN?
options: Its lines do not rhyme at all.
It contains three lines rather than two.
It necessarily uses six iambic feet.
Its grammatical sense ends with the second line.
questions.explanation: Closure depends on completed syntax at the end of the pair, not on a particular subject or change of meter.

questions.question: A four-line stanza rhymes ABAB. A student calls lines 1–2 and 3–4 two rhymed couplets. Why is that classification wrong?
options: Couplets cannot form part of a four-line stanza.
An ABAB stanza contains no end rhyme at all.
A couplet must always be six lines long.
Neither adjacent pair rhymes internally; each A rhymes with a nonadjacent A, and likewise for B.
questions.explanation: The defining paired end rhymes would be AA and BB, not the alternating pattern ABAB.

questions.question: What is the defining line count of a tercet?
questions.explanation: A tercet is a unit of three poetic lines, whether rhymed or unrhymed.

questions.question: Which pattern can be used by a rhymed tercet?
questions.explanation: A three-line unit may use a single shared end rhyme, giving the pattern AAA.

questions.question: A poet places three lines together, with lines 1 and 3 rhyming while line 2 differs. What is the unit and pattern?
questions.explanation: Three lines make a tercet; matching first and third endings produce ABA.

questions.question: In terza rima, a first tercet rhymes ABA. Which scheme must the next interlocking tercet take?
questions.explanation: Terza rima carries the previous stanza’s middle-line rhyme into the first and third lines of the next tercet.

questions.question: How many lines are in a quatrain?
questions.explanation: A quatrain is a four-line stanza, and it can use several different rhyme patterns.

questions.question: Which name is commonly given to the ABBA quatrain rhyme pattern?
questions.explanation: ABBA encloses the inner BB pair within matching A end sounds.

questions.question: In a typical ABCB ballad quatrain, which lines rhyme with one another?
questions.explanation: In ABCB the B rhyme recurs on lines 2 and 4; lines 1 and 3 do not rhyme with those or each other.

questions.question: Two quatrains have schemes ABBA and ABAB. Which comparison is correct?
options: ABBA encloses a central pair; ABAB alternates two rhymes.
Both are examples of AABB paired rhyme.
ABAB lacks any matching end sounds.
ABBA requires five lines, unlike ABAB.
questions.explanation: ABBA places A around two B lines, whereas ABAB alternates A and B across four lines.

questions.question: How many lines are in a traditional rhyme-royal stanza?
questions.explanation: Rhyme royal is a seven-line stanza typically written in iambic pentameter.

questions.question: Which end-rhyme pattern is standard for rhyme royal?
questions.explanation: Rhyme royal follows ABABBCC, with a final CC couplet.

questions.question: Which medieval English poet famously employed rhyme royal in Troilus and Criseyde?
questions.explanation: Chaucer helped establish the seven-line ABABBCC stanza in English narrative poetry.

questions.question: A seven-line stanza has rhyme scheme ABABBCC. How many distinct rhyme sounds are present, and which lines form the closing couplet?
questions.explanation: A, B, and C are the three rhyme families; C appears twice at the end, in lines 6 and 7.

questions.question: A student writes seven lines rhyming ABABBCC, but all lines are regular iambic tetrameter. What is the most precise assessment?
options: The rhyme pattern matches rhyme royal, but its customary ten-syllable pentameter lines are absent.
It must be a Spenserian stanza because it ends in CC.
It is fully standard rhyme royal because the form requires tetrameter.
It must be ottava rima, since that form has seven lines.
questions.explanation: Standard English rhyme royal uses seven iambic-pentameter lines; its ABABBCC rhyme pattern alone does not reproduce the usual metrical form.

questions.question: How many lines make up an ottava-rima stanza?
questions.explanation: Ottava rima is an eight-line stanza imported into English from Italian verse.

questions.question: Which rhyme scheme belongs to ottava rima?
questions.explanation: Ottava rima alternates two rhymes over six lines and closes with a CC couplet.

questions.question: Which major English-language poem uses ottava rima for extended comic and satirical narration?
questions.explanation: Byron adapted the eight-line ABABABCC form for the witty, digressive narrative of Don Juan.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes ottava rima from rhyme royal when both end with a rhyming couplet?
options: Ottava rima has eight lines and ABABABCC; rhyme royal has seven and ABABBCC.
Ottava rima ends in DD; rhyme royal never ends in a couplet.
Ottava rima has seven lines; rhyme royal has eight.
Ottava rima is always unrhymed, while rhyme royal is rhymed.
questions.explanation: Both are rhymed stanzas that close in a couplet, but their line counts and preceding rhyme sequences differ.

questions.question: An eight-line draft is labelled ABABACCC. Which SINGLE revision makes its scheme exactly ottava rima?
options: Change line 8 from C to B.
Change line 5 from A to C.
Change line 6 from rhyme C to rhyme B.
Change line 7 from C to A.
questions.explanation: ABABACCC becomes ABABABCC when the sixth line adopts rhyme B; the final two lines remain CC.

questions.question: How many lines are in a Spenserian stanza?
questions.explanation: The Spenserian stanza contains nine rhymed lines, the last of which is longer than the first eight.

questions.question: Which work by Edmund Spenser is especially associated with the Spenserian stanza?
questions.explanation: Spenser developed this interlaced nine-line stanza in The Faerie Queene.

questions.question: What is the traditional rhyme scheme of the Spenserian stanza?
questions.explanation: Its nine-line rhyme scheme is ABABBCBCC, with interlocking B and C sounds.

questions.question: What metrical change occurs in the ninth line of a standard Spenserian stanza?
options: A rhymed couplet replaces the ninth line entirely.
An alexandrine of six iambic feet replaces the preceding iambic-pentameter lines.
A seven-foot trochaic line replaces the preceding blank verse.
A three-foot iambic line replaces eight lines of hexameter.
questions.explanation: The first eight lines are iambic pentameter; the ninth is an alexandrine, or iambic hexameter.

questions.question: In the scheme ABABBCBCC, which four line positions share the B rhyme?
questions.explanation: Reading ABABBCBCC from left to right, B occurs at positions 2, 4, 5, and 7.
